slot.brief: Ask which indicator/apparatus is correct for a strong acid–strong base titration and why the burette is rinsed with the titrant first.

stem: During the titration of a strong acid with a strong base, the burette is rinsed with the titrant after washing with water. This is done to:
options: prevent dilution of the titrant by residual water
remove air bubbles trapped inside the burette tip
neutralize acidic or basic residues on the glass
facilitate smooth delivery of liquid from the stopcock

verdicts.working: Water left after washing dilutes the titrant, lowering its effective concentration (~1% error for 0.5 mL residual water in 50 mL of 0.1 M titrant) and causing titre errors. Rinsing with titrant replaces the water film so concentration stays exact. Air bubbles are removed by draining, not rinsing; C and D are not the purpose.

working:
In volumetric analysis, after washing the burette with distilled water, droplets of water remain adhering to the interior glass walls. If the titrant is introduced directly, this residual water will dilute the titrant, decreasing its concentration and leading to an overestimation of the titre value. Rinsing the burette with small portions of the titrant solution coats the walls with the titrant itself, ensuring that the concentration of the solution placed in the burette remains strictly unaltered.

draft.distractor_notes:
Option B confuses the pre-rinse with the subsequent step of opening the stopcock fully to expel air bubbles from the jet tip.
Option C incorrectly treats rinsing with titrant as a cleaning/neutralization step; residues must be removed beforehand by proper washing.
Option D confuses chemical rinsing with the mechanical operation or lubrication of the stopcock.
